name: Testing Examples
summary: Free open source HTML fixtures for practicing browser automation, plus 47 sibling demo repos that exercise them.
description: The home page is a deliberately plain, stable page of elements with known ids, names, classes, link text, lists, and form inputs, meant to be found by Selenium WebDriver, WebdriverIO, Playwright, and similar tools. Of the 47 sibling repositories, 12 are generic-target locator-strategy walkthroughs that drive a browser directly against this site's home page; five of those twelve additionally have this site's fixture markup (the ids, names, classes, and text under "Id Examples" through "Form Input Examples") as a contract they depend on exactly. Eleven more sibling repos drive the same kinds of tools against a real public site, nhs.wales, instead, and do not depend on this site's markup. The remaining 24 pair the same tools and languages against Google Search or Google Maps, illustratively only, and are never executed against the live sites — see /locales/en-001/about/ for the complete table. Every page below is also available in five more locales — English (UK), English (UK, Oxford spelling), English (US), Welsh (UK), and Welsh (international) — at /locales/<locale>/; the links below are the default locale, English (international, en-001). See spec/locales/index.md.

sections.title: Learn
sections.description: What automatic testing is and how to get started with browser automation tools.

links.title: What is automatic testing?
links.description: What automatic testing is, and how it differs from and complements manual testing.

links.title: What is the purpose of automatic testing?
links.description: What a team actually gets back for the effort of writing automatic tests — earlier bugs, tireless repetition, and the confidence to release often.

links.title: What is the automatic testing pyramid?
links.description: The three layers of automatic tests, from fast, cheap unit tests at the base to realistic end-to-end browser tests at the top.

links.title: What is browser automatic testing?
links.description: What it is, and the trade-offs that come with its realism — slower, more brittle, and harder to diagnose than a unit test.

links.title: What is continuous integration automatic testing?
links.description: Running your automatic test suite automatically on every change, so broken code is caught before it merges rather than after.

links.title: How to start learning automatic testing?
links.description: A step-by-step path — pick a language, pick a tool, run a first script against this site, then practice on real examples.

links.title: How does artificial intelligence help automatic testing?
links.description: How and why AI shows up in writing tests, CI/CD, and agile discovery today, and the caveat that applies to all three.

links.title: What are related concepts for automatic testing?
links.description: Friendly introductions to code editors, version control (git and GitHub), and agile discovery.

sections.title: Learn More
sections.description: Bonus topics extracted from the related concepts page.

links.title: What is DevOps for automatic testing?
links.description: What DevOps is, and why testing in production legitimately complements pre-release testing rather than replacing it.

links.title: What metrics help automatic testing?
links.description: Cycle time, lead time, throughput, and work in progress, and why a growing pile of flaky tests is itself a flow-metric signal.

links.title: How does Six Sigma lead manual testing into automatic testing?
links.description: Lean and Six Sigma, and why a flaky test is literally "variation" worth root-causing rather than re-running until it goes green.
